# Writing an Engineering Article

Write for an engineer who was not in the conversation. Explain the causal chain:
what made the problem difficult, what mattered in choosing an approach, how the
approach works, and what the available outcome actually supports.

- Open with the concrete problem and constraints, not a recap of who spoke when.
- Explain real alternatives discussed and why an option was selected, rejected,
  or deferred. Do not invent a comparison to make the decision look rigorous.
- Preserve authorship: distinguish a human choice, a Navigator suggestion, and
  Driver implementation. A suggestion is not a decision until accepted. Retain
  rejected advice and changes of mind when they explain the result.
- Name the accepted costs and conditions under which the choice would change.
  A local trade-off is not a universal best practice.
- Explain mechanisms with concrete technical detail supported by the context.
  Use small code excerpts only when necessary; avoid dumping logs or transcripts.
- Separate what was changed from what was verified. Attribute reported test
  results as reports. Failed, incomplete, and not-run checks stay that way.
- State missing context and uncertainty near the affected claim. Do not turn
  partial evidence into a polished success story or infer motives from code.
- End with a bounded lesson the reader can reuse, including its conditions and
  unresolved questions. Never score the user's competence or approve Driver work.

Choose a specific title and a few headings suited to this task, not a fixed
checklist. A short, well-supported article is better than padded sections. Keep
the reasoning readable in prose; use a list or table only when it clarifies a
real comparison. No marketing claims, generic takeaways, or mandatory word count.
